Run a test command and return an adjudicated verdict, not test output

Usage:
  entire graph verify --test "<cmd>" --repo . [--setup "<cmd>"] [--record-baseline path | --pre-edit-baseline path] [--max-bytes 2048]

verify runs your test command and reports WHICH TESTS CHANGED rather than what the runner printed: which newly pass, which newly fail, and which were ALREADY failing before the edit (labelled PRE-EXISTING). Raw runner output is never forwarded — ids are, text is not — and id lists cap at 20 with a count.

Record a baseline on the pristine tree first (--record-baseline), then pass that file as --pre-edit-baseline after editing. Without a baseline the verdict is a state rather than a delta, so a failure that predates the change cannot be labelled as one.

Parsers: pytest, jest/vitest, cargo test, go test, phpunit, rspec, minitest, maven/gradle surefire, ctest. An unrecognised format degrades to an exit-code-only verdict and says so.

Flags:
  --test <cmd>                 The test command to run (required)
  --repo <path>                Repository to run in (default: current repo)
  --setup <cmd>                Command run before the tests; its output never contributes test ids
  --record-baseline <path>     Write the pristine-tree result to this file instead of adjudicating
  --pre-edit-baseline <path>   Diff this run against a previously recorded baseline
  --max-bytes <n>              Cap the rendered verdict; the verdict clause always survives (default: 2048)

Examples:
  entire graph verify --repo . --test "pytest tests/test_parser.py" --record-baseline /tmp/base.json
  entire graph verify --repo . --test "pytest tests/test_parser.py" --pre-edit-baseline /tmp/base.json

Explain provides human-readable context about sessions, commits, and checkpoints.

Use this command to understand what happened during agent-driven development,
either for self-review or to understand a teammate's work.

By default, shows checkpoints on the current branch. Pass a checkpoint ID or
commit SHA as a positional argument to explain a specific item, or use flags.

Viewing specific items:
  entire checkpoint explain <id-or-sha>           Auto-detects checkpoint ID or commit SHA
  entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <id>     Force interpretation as checkpoint ID
  entire checkpoint explain --commit <ref>        Force interpretation as commit ref

Checkpoints in another repo:
  entire checkpoint explain <id> --repo gh/owner/name
  entire checkpoint explain <id> --repo et/project/repo
                 Explain a checkpoint owned by another repository — the
                 drill-down for a cross-repo 'entire search' hit. Reads it from
                 that repo's Entire API; nothing is written to this repo.
                 Needs a full checkpoint ID (positional or --checkpoint) and a
                 checkpoint that has been pushed.

Filtering the list view:
  --session      Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)

Output verbosity levels (when explaining a specific item):
  Default:         Detailed view with scoped prompts (ID, session, tokens, intent, prompts, files)
  --short          Summary only (ID, session, timestamp, tokens, intent)
  --full           Parsed full transcript (all prompts/responses from entire session)
  --raw-transcript Raw transcript file (JSONL format)

Machine-readable export modes (additive surface for external consumers):
  --json           Metadata-only JSON. Lists checkpoints when no target is given;
                   emits a single checkpoint envelope when a target is supplied,
                   including its subagent task records under "tasks".
                   Transcript bytes are NEVER embedded in the JSON envelope.
  --transcript     Stream stored checkpoint transcript bytes (JSONL) to stdout
                   for the selected session. Same bytes as --raw-transcript
                   while checkpoints v1 is the checkpoint store.
  --session-index  Pick a session within a multi-session checkpoint (0-based).
                   Defaults to the latest session. Only meaningful with
                   --transcript or --raw-transcript.
  --task           With --transcript, stream a subagent's stored transcript
                   instead, selected by tool_use_id or agent_id (as listed
                   under "tasks" in --json).
  --limit          Cap the number of checkpoints returned by the list view.
                   Defaults to 100. When the cap is hit, a stderr note
                   says how many were skipped. Only meaningful with --json.

Summary generation:
  --generate    Generate an AI summary for the checkpoint. This is the only
                part of this command that writes: it stores the summary on the
                checkpoint and spends tokens with the configured summary
                provider. Every other mode only reads.
  --force       Regenerate even if a summary already exists (requires --generate)

Performance options:
  --search-all  Remove branch/depth limits when searching for commits (may be slow)

Checkpoint detail view shows:
  - Author of the checkpoint
  - Associated git commits that reference the checkpoint
  - Prompts and responses from the session

Note: --session filters the list view; the positional arg, --commit, and --checkpoint are mutually exclusive.

Usage:
  entire checkpoint explain [checkpoint-id | commit-sha] [flags]

Flags:
  -c, --checkpoint string             Explain a specific checkpoint (ID or prefix)
      --commit string                 Explain a specific commit (SHA or ref, "commit-ish")
      --force                         Regenerate summary even if one already exists (requires --generate)
      --full                          Show full parsed transcript (all prompts/responses)
      --generate                      Generate an AI summary for the checkpoint
  -h, --help                          help for explain
      --insecure-http-auth            Allow plain-HTTP auth for --repo (local dev only)
      --json                          Output metadata as JSON (no transcript bytes)
      --limit int                     Cap the list view at N checkpoints (default: 100). Only meaningful with --json.
      --no-pager                      Disable pager output
      --raw-transcript                Show raw transcript file (JSONL format)
      --repo string                   Explain a checkpoint owned by another repo (gh/owner/name, et/project/repo, entire://<host>/gh/<owner>/<repo>, or entire://<host>/et/<project>/<repo>), read from that repo's Entire API
      --search-all                    Search all commits (no branch/depth limit, may be slow)
      --session string                Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)
      --session-index int             Session index within a multi-session checkpoint (0-based, defaults to latest) (default -1)
  -s, --short                         Show summary only (omit prompts and files)
      --summary-timeout-seconds int   Hard deadline in seconds for --generate summary generation; overrides summary_timeout_seconds setting. 0 = use setting; if setting is also unset or 0, no automatic deadline applies.
      --task string                   Subagent task (tool_use_id or agent_id) whose stored transcript --transcript streams
      --transcript                    Stream stored checkpoint transcript bytes to stdout (a session's, or a subagent's with --task)

Global Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only — including the git and agent processes it spawns — instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

This needs a small schema-safe design choice: rather than inventing a new row type, I’ll use a ledger row with `attempt: 2`, same task, `handoff: entire-handoff`, zero ceiling, model/harness marked as Entire, and a decision explaining it is the handoff summary cost. That keeps existing schema and dashboard readers valid while making the spend visible.

One caveat I’m keeping visible: the schema currently says “attempt” rows only, so the handoff-cost row has to look like a zero-ceiling failed/passed attempt-style row unless we change schema. I’ll keep it valid and explicit in `decision`/`resultReason`, and avoid touching dashboard/schema beyond the necessary fields.

gh pr create --base main --head ao/neatlogs-hack-5/e5-e7-entire-checkpoints --title "Record Entire checkpoint evidence on escalations" --body $'## Summary
- add an Entire checkpoint/handoff adapter that finds session evidence from `entire session info`, pending logs-only checkpoints, condensed checkpoints, or commit trailers
- record checkpoint ids on real worker attempt ledger rows when Entire is enabled; leave checkpointUrl null unless Entire returns one
- pass the failed branch and checkpoint summary into the escalation prompt and support a separate handoff-summary ledger cost row when the provider reports summary spend

## Live check
- `entire checkpoint list --pending --json` shows Codex sessions with `session_id` and logs-only `condensation_id`, which explains why prior rows were null: Tally never queried Entire after workers finished.
- `entire checkpoint explain <id> --json` returns `checkpoint_id`, branch, files touched, and session metadata, but no dashboard URL.
- `entire checkpoint explain <id> --generate` currently fails locally with Claude auth (`Please run /login`), so real summary-generation cost is not exposed; the engine records a separate ledger row when the handoff port does provide summary cost/tokens and otherwise avoids fabricating spend.

## Tests
- `npx vitest run adapters/entire-checkpoints.test.ts agent/escalation.test.ts engine/real.test.ts`
- `npm run -s typecheck`
- `npm run -s build`

- `npm run -s build`

# CrustData D1 spike findings

Date: 2026-10-10
Scope: read-only API probing with `CRUSTDATA_API_KEY` from `~/.tally/.env`. The key was not printed or copied.

## Documentation checked

- CrustData documents `POST https://api.crustdata.com/company/search` with `Authorization: Bearer ...`, `content-type: application/json`, and `x-api-version: 2025-11-01`.
- Public docs say Company Search returns `companies`, `next_cursor`, and `total_count`, and prices search at `0.03 credits per result` on the product page. The live response headers reported higher per-call credit figures for this account/path; see below.
- Docs/product pages say Company Search supports firmographic, headcount, hiring, job-listing, employee-skill and keyword style filters, but the live API rejected some advertised fields as conditions.

Sources:
- https://crustdata.com/company-data-api
- https://crustdata.com/apis/company-discovery
- https://www.crustdata.com/blog/company-search-api

## Calls made

All calls used `POST /company/search`, `x-api-version: 2025-11-01`, and tiny `limit` values.

1. Basic company search, valid

Payload shape:

```json
{
  "filters": {
    "op": "and",
    "conditions": [
      { "field": "headcount.total", "type": ">", "value": 50 }
    ]
  },
  "fields": ["basic_info.name", "basic_info.primary_domain", "headcount.total"],
  "limit": 1
}
```

Result:

- HTTP 200.
- Top-level keys: `companies`, `next_cursor`, `total_count`.
- Example returned company: `a2z Infrastructure (P) Ltd`, domain `a2zgroup.co.in`, headcount `321`.
- `total_count`: `994745`.
- Response header `x-credit-cost`: `0.43`.

2. Basic company search with hiring fields returned, valid

Payload shape:

```json
{
  "filters": {
    "op": "and",
    "conditions": [
      { "field": "headcount.total", "type": "=>", "value": 51 },
      { "field": "headcount.total", "type": "=<", "value": 500 }
    ]
  },
  "fields": [
    "basic_info.name",
    "basic_info.primary_domain",
    "basic_info.description",
    "headcount.total",
    "hiring.openings_count",
    "hiring.by_function_6m_pct.engineering",
    "taxonomy.professional_network_industry"
  ],
  "limit": 1
}
```

Result:

- HTTP 200.
- Same company came back because the filter is broad.
- `hiring` was `null` for that company, but the fields were accepted as return fields.
- `taxonomy.professional_network_industry` returned `Oil and Gas`.
- `total_count`: `891820`.
- Response header `x-credit-cost`: `0.53`.

3. Invalid/zero-credit probes

The API returned useful validation errors and reported `x-credit-cost: 0` for these rejected requests:

- `taxonomy.industry` is not a valid return field. The API suggested `taxonomy` or `taxonomy.professional_network_industry`.
- `between` is not a valid comparison operator in the live endpoint despite examples using it. The API accepts `=>` and `=<` for lower/upper bounds.
- `query` is a return field but is not supported as a filter condition.
- `hiring.openings_count` and `hiring.by_function_6m_pct.engineering` are accepted as return fields but were rejected as condition fields in this endpoint/account.
- A guessed `company_keywords` condition did not get a fair test because the request also had the invalid taxonomy return field; I did not spend another call after the stricter field errors were clear.

## Can we list engineering teams adopting coding agents?

Not directly from this spike alone.

What works:

- Company Search can return structured company lists with domains, descriptions, headcount, taxonomy and selected hiring fields.
- The API exposes an `available_fields` list in validation metadata that includes hiring fields such as `hiring.openings_count`, `hiring.by_function_6m_pct.engineering`, and `hiring.by_function_qoq_pct.engineering`.
- A D2 implementation can reliably save and rerun exact structured company-search payloads.

What did not work in the live probes:

- Free-text `query` could not be used as a condition.
- Engineering hiring fields could not be used as conditions in `POST /company/search`; they appear returnable but not filterable through this endpoint/account.
- I did not find a confirmed condition field for “uses Cursor/Copilot/Codex/coding agents” without either docs for keyword filters or an enrichment/search endpoint that accepts natural-language queries.

Likely D2 path:

1. Use `/company/search` for the structured company universe: e.g. headcount range, country, software/technology taxonomy where valid, and return `basic_info.description`, `hiring.*`, `taxonomy.*`.
2. For “adopting coding agents,” add a second stage if available: either CrustData MCP/natural-language search, a realtime search endpoint that accepts keyword filters, or enrichment fields/posts/jobs that can be searched for terms like `Cursor`, `GitHub Copilot`, `Codex`, `AI coding assistant`, `developer productivity`, and `agentic coding`.
3. Until a keyword/natural-language condition is verified, label D2 as “companies with engineering/hiring signals plus coding-agent keyword evidence” only when that evidence comes from a returned text field or a separate verified endpoint.

## Credit cost observed

- Successful returned-row calls: `0.43 + 0.53 = 0.96` credits by response header.
- Rejected validation calls: `0` credits by response header.
- This differs from the public product page statement of `0.03 credits per result`, so D2 should record response headers for actual cost accounting.

```json
      { "field": "headcount.total", "type": "=>", "value": 51 },
      { "field": "headcount.total", "type": "=<", "value": 500 }
    ]
  },
  "fields": [
    "basic_info.name",
    "basic_info.primary_domain",
    "basic_info.description",
    "headcount.total",
    "hiring.openings_count",
    "hiring.by_function_6m_pct.engineering",
    "taxonomy.professional_network_industry"
  ],
  "limit": 1
}
```

Result:

- HTTP 200.
- Same company came back because the filter is broad.
- `hiring` was `null` for that company, but the fields were accepted as return fields.
- `taxonomy.professional_network_industry` returned `Oil and Gas`.
- `total_count`: `891820`.
- Response header `x-credit-cost`: `0.53`.

3. Invalid/zero-credit probes

The API returned useful validation errors and reported `x-credit-cost: 0` for these rejected requests:

- `taxonomy.industry` is not a valid return field. The API suggested `taxonomy` or `taxonomy.professional_network_industry`.
- `between` is not a valid comparison operator in the live endpoint despite examples using it. The API accepts `=>` and `=<` for lower/upper bounds.
- `query` is a return field but is not supported as a filter condition.
- `hiring.openings_count` and `hiring.by_function_6m_pct.engineering` are accepted as return fields but were rejected as condition fields in this endpoint/account.
- A guessed `company_keywords` condition did not get a fair test because the request also had the invalid taxonomy return field; I did not spend another call after the stricter field errors were clear.

## Can we list engineering teams adopting coding agents?

Not directly from this spike alone.

What works:

- Company Search can return structured company lists with domains, descriptions, headcount, taxonomy and selected hiring fields.
- The API exposes an `available_fields` list in validation metadata that includes hiring fields such as `hiring.openings_count`, `hiring.by_function_6m_pct.engineering`, and `hiring.by_function_qoq_pct.engineering`.
- A D2 implementation can reliably save and rerun exact structured company-search payloads.

What did not work in the live probes:

- Free-text `query` could not be used as a condition.
- Engineering hiring fields could not be used as conditions in `POST /company/search`; they appear returnable but not filterable through this endpoint/account.
- I did not find a confirmed condition field for “uses Cursor/Copilot/Codex/coding agents” without either docs for keyword filters or an enrichment/search endpoint that accepts natural-language queries.

Likely D2 path:

1. Use `/company/search` for the structured company universe: e.g. headcount range, country, software/technology taxonomy where valid, and return `basic_info.description`, `hiring.*`, `taxonomy.*`.
2. For “adopting coding agents,” add a second stage if available: either CrustData MCP/natural-language search, a realtime search endpoint that accepts keyword filters, or enrichment fields/posts/jobs that can be searched for terms like `Cursor`, `GitHub Copilot`, `Codex`, `AI coding assistant`, `developer productivity`, and `agentic coding`.
3. Until a keyword/natural-language condition is verified, label D2 as “companies with engineering/hiring signals plus coding-agent keyword evidence” only when that evidence comes from a returned text field or a separate verified endpoint.

## Credit cost observed

- Successful returned-row calls: `0.43 + 0.53 = 0.96` credits by response header.
- Rejected validation calls: `0` credits by response header.
- This differs from the public product page statement of `0.03 credits per result`, so D2 should record response headers for actual cost accounting.

Filesystem sandboxing defines which files can be read or written. `sandbox_mode` is `workspace-write`: The sandbox permits reading files, and editing files in `cwd` and `writable_roots`. Editing files in other directories requires approval. Network access is restricted.
# Escalation Requests

Commands are run outside the sandbox if they are approved by the user, or match an existing rule that allows it to run unrestricted. The command string is split into independent command segments at shell control operators, including but not limited to:

- Pipes: |
- Logical operators: &&, ||
- Command separators: ;
- Subshell boundaries: (...), $(...)

Each resulting segment is evaluated independently for sandbox restrictions and approval requirements.

Example:

git pull | tee output.txt

This is treated as two command segments:

["git", "pull"]

["tee", "output.txt"]

Commands that use more advanced shell features like redirection (>, >>, <), substitutions ($(...), ...), environment variables (FOO=bar), or wildcard patterns (*, ?) will not be evaluated against rules, to limit the scope of what an approved rule allows.

## How to request escalation

IMPORTANT: To request approval to execute a command that will require escalated privileges:

- Provide the `sandbox_permissions` parameter with the value `"require_escalated"`
- Include a short question asking the user if they want to allow the action in `justification` parameter. e.g. "Do you want to download and install dependencies for this project?"
- Optionally suggest a `prefix_rule` - this will be shown to the user with an option to persist the rule approval for future sessions.

If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with "require_escalated". ALWAYS proceed to use the `justification` parameter - do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.

## When to request escalation

While commands are running inside the sandbox, here are some scenarios that will require escalation outside the sandbox:

- You need to run a command that writes to a directory that requires it (e.g. running tests that write to /var)

## prefix_rule guidance

When choosing a `prefix_rule`, request one that will allow you to fulfill similar requests from the user in the future without re-requesting escalation. It should be categorical and reasonably scoped to similar capabilities. You should rarely pass the entire command into `prefix_rule`.

---
name: using-ao
description: "Catalog of the AO (Agent Orchestrator) `ao` CLI: spawning workers, managing sessions and projects, creating reusable Cues, sending messages, controlling the shared browser, previewing pages, and daemon control. Use when using the ao CLI, creating Cues, spawning workers, or managing AO sessions in an AO workspace."
trigger: "Using the ao CLI in an AO workspace: creating Cues, spawning workers, managing sessions/projects, sending messages, controlling or previewing pages."
---

# AO CLI Catalog

`ao` is a thin CLI over the local AO daemon. Every command is `ao <command> --help` for the authoritative flag list.

| Command | What it does | When to use | Details |
|---|---|---|---|

# ao report

Persist a meaningful worker report for durable delivery to the active project
orchestrator.

## Syntax

```text
ao report <free-form-text>
ao report --checkpoint --note <text> [output flags]
ao report --needs-input --note <text> [output flags]
ao report --stuck --note <text> [output flags]
ao report --done --note <text> [output flags]
```

Output flags are repeatable:

```text
--artifact <opaque-reference>
--pr-created <pr-or-mr-url>
--pr-reviewed <pr-or-mr-url>
```

Use reports for meaningful transitions, decisions, blockers, required input,
outputs, and terminal judgment. Do not narrate routine commands. Outputs do not
imply completion, and `--done` does not terminate the session.

Attach a reviewable deliverable as soon as it is ready, not only at `--done`:
use `--artifact <reference>` on the report for the milestone that produced it.
Examples include a requested document, a rendered dashboard, or another output
the orchestrator or human needs to open directly. `--artifact` takes any opaque
reference string; it is not validated as a URL.
In a chat session, an HTML file from the artifact directory that you attach
with `--artifact` also shows in the thread.

Routine test logs, command output, scratch notes, and intermediate diagnostics
are working material, not deliverables. Do not attach them unless requested or
needed to explain an actionable failure. Summarize validation in the report note;
when a separate deliverable is useful, prefer one consolidated report over
individual logs. Ordinary progress updates and concise final answers do not
need separate artifact files.

Saving a local artifact or attaching its reference to an AO report is not
external publishing authorization. Publish externally only within the
user-authorized scope.

`--pr-created` and `--pr-reviewed` accept complete GitHub PR or GitLab MR URLs.

`--needs-input` requests immediate non-interrupting delivery. `--stuck`
requests immediate delivery plus a rate-limited interrupt. Informational work
batches for up to one hour, while the first done report opens a fixed five
minute settlement window.

**Examples:**

```bash
ao report "The focused tests pass; I am checking the generated diff."
ao report --done --note "Ready for review." \
  --pr-created https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/88
```

# AO CLI Catalog

`ao` is a thin CLI over the local AO daemon. Every command is `ao <command> --help` for the authoritative flag list.

| Command | What it does | When to use | Details |
|---|---|---|---|
| `spawn` | Spawn a project worker, orchestrator, or projectless standalone worker | Starting a new task or issue | [commands/spawn.md](commands/spawn.md) |
| `session` | Manage agent sessions (list, kill, rename, restore, etc.) | Inspecting or controlling running/terminated sessions | [commands/session.md](commands/session.md) |
| `agent` | Inspect installed harnesses and launch readiness | Choosing or diagnosing an agent harness | `ao agent ls --refresh` |
| `pr` | Merge a PR or resolve its review threads | Completing a reviewed change | `ao pr merge` / `ao pr resolve-comments` |
| `project` | Register, inspect, configure, or remove projects | Setting up or managing repos AO knows about | [commands/project.md](commands/project.md) |
| `automation` | Manage durable recurring session automations | Creating, editing, disabling, deleting, and inspecting scheduled runs | [commands/automation.md](commands/automation.md) |
| `cue` | Create or list reusable project Cues | Saving a repetitive command or agent task at the user's request | [commands/cue.md](commands/cue.md) |
| `orchestrator` | List orchestrator sessions | Viewing which sessions are orchestrators | [commands/orchestrator.md](commands/orchestrator.md) |
| `review` | Start, list, cancel, or submit AO's native reviewer for a worker's PR (default: this session) | Getting an adversarial review of an AO session's PR; never spawn a worker to review | [commands/review.md](commands/review.md) |
| `send` | Send a message to a running agent session | Correcting or directing a live agent | [commands/send.md](commands/send.md) |
| `report` | Persist a meaningful worker report | Checkpoints, blockers, decisions, outputs, and completion | [commands/report.md](commands/report.md) |
| `preview` | Start a session-owned app or open an exact URL/file | Running and showing the worker's relevant app, Markdown, HTML, PDF, or image | [commands/preview.md](commands/preview.md) |
| `render` | Show a self-contained HTML page inline in a chat thread | Answering with a chart, table, diagram, or mockup | [commands/render.md](commands/render.md) |
| `browser` | Inspect and control the session's shared live browser | Verifying a web app through snapshots, interactions, waits, screenshots, console, and errors | [commands/browser.md](commands/browser.md) |
| `start` | Fetch (if needed) and open the AO desktop app | Launching the app | [commands/start.md](commands/start.md) |
| `stop` | Stop the AO daemon | Shutting down AO | [commands/stop.md](commands/stop.md) |
| `status` | Show daemon status | Verifying the daemon is up and healthy | [commands/status.md](commands/status.md) |
| `doctor` | Run local health checks | Diagnosing AO setup problems | [commands/doctor.md](commands/doctor.md) |
| `import` | Import projects from a legacy AO install | Migrating from the old flat-file store | [commands/import.md](commands/import.md) |
| `version` | Print version information | Checking installed version | - |
| `completion` | Generate shell completion scripts | Setting up tab completion | - |

## Conventions

- Most read commands accept `--json` for machine-readable output.
- `-p / --project` scopes session subcommand lookups to one project.
- Session and project ids are shown by `ao session ls` and `ao project ls`.
- To refer to a session in AO Chat or the AO terminal, use the canonical in-app
  link `ao://sessions/{project-id}/{session-id}`. Read
  [commands/session.md](commands/session.md) for identity, encoding, and safety
  rules before constructing one.
- When the user asks to save a repeatable task as a Cue, use `ao cue list --json` to check existing definitions, then `ao cue create`. An agent Cue stores a reusable instruction; a command Cue stores an exact shell command. This agent-facing command can create and read Cues, but cannot edit or delete them. Direct the user to project settings for changes to existing Cues.
- `--agent` is an alias for `--harness` on `ao spawn`.
- Every command accepts `-h / --help` for the full flag list.
- For frontend launch, preview selection, or artifact handoff, read
  [commands/preview.md](commands/preview.md) before acting. Its static-file,
  project-runtime, and automatic-handoff rules are load-bearing.
- For page inspection, interaction, or request diagnosis, read
  [commands/browser.md](commands/browser.md). It defines shared-tab behavior
  and the opt-in network policy.

Use [references.md](references.md) only when a natural-language request does
not map clearly to a command above.

# ao report

Persist a meaningful worker report for durable delivery to the active project
orchestrator.

## Syntax

```text
ao report <free-form-text>
ao report --checkpoint --note <text> [output flags]
ao report --needs-input --note <text> [output flags]
ao report --stuck --note <text> [output flags]
ao report --done --note <text> [output flags]
```

Output flags are repeatable:

```text
--artifact <opaque-reference>
--pr-created <pr-or-mr-url>
--pr-reviewed <pr-or-mr-url>
```

Use reports for meaningful transitions, decisions, blockers, required input,
outputs, and terminal judgment. Do not narrate routine commands. Outputs do not
imply completion, and `--done` does not terminate the session.

Attach a reviewable deliverable as soon as it is ready, not only at `--done`:
use `--artifact <reference>` on the report for the milestone that produced it.
Examples include a requested document, a rendered dashboard, or another output
the orchestrator or human needs to open directly. `--artifact` takes any opaque
reference string; it is not validated as a URL.
In a chat session, an HTML file from the artifact directory that you attach
with `--artifact` also shows in the thread.

Routine test logs, command output, scratch notes, and intermediate diagnostics
are working material, not deliverables. Do not attach them unless requested or
needed to explain an actionable failure. Summarize validation in the report note;
when a separate deliverable is useful, prefer one consolidated report over
individual logs. Ordinary progress updates and concise final answers do not
need separate artifact files.

Saving a local artifact or attaching its reference to an AO report is not
external publishing authorization. Publish externally only within the
user-authorized scope.

`--pr-created` and `--pr-reviewed` accept complete GitHub PR or GitLab MR URLs.

`--needs-input` requests immediate non-interrupting delivery. `--stuck`
requests immediate delivery plus a rate-limited interrupt. Informational work
batches for up to one hour, while the first done report opens a fixed five
minute settlement window.

**Examples:**

```bash
ao report "The focused tests pass; I am checking the generated diff."
ao report --done --note "Ready for review." \
  --pr-created https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/88
```

name: using-ao
description: "Catalog of the AO (Agent Orchestrator) `ao` CLI: spawning workers, managing sessions and projects, creating reusable Cues, sending messages, controlling the shared browser, previewing pages, and daemon control. Use when using the ao CLI, creating Cues, spawning workers, or managing AO sessions in an AO workspace."
trigger: "Using the ao CLI in an AO workspace: creating Cues, spawning workers, managing sessions/projects, sending messages, controlling or previewing pages."
---

# AO CLI Catalog

`ao` is a thin CLI over the local AO daemon. Every command is `ao <command> --help` for the authoritative flag list.

| Command | What it does | When to use | Details |
|---|---|---|---|
| `spawn` | Spawn a project worker, orchestrator, or projectless standalone worker | Starting a new task or issue | [commands/spawn.md](commands/spawn.md) |
| `session` | Manage agent sessions (list, kill, rename, restore, etc.) | Inspecting or controlling running/terminated sessions | [commands/session.md](commands/session.md) |
| `agent` | Inspect installed harnesses and launch readiness | Choosing or diagnosing an agent harness | `ao agent ls --refresh` |
| `pr` | Merge a PR or resolve its review threads | Completing a reviewed change | `ao pr merge` / `ao pr resolve-comments` |
| `project` | Register, inspect, configure, or remove projects | Setting up or managing repos AO knows about | [commands/project.md](commands/project.md) |
| `automation` | Manage durable recurring session automations | Creating, editing, disabling, deleting, and inspecting scheduled runs | [commands/automation.md](commands/automation.md) |
| `cue` | Create or list reusable project Cues | Saving a repetitive command or agent task at the user's request | [commands/cue.md](commands/cue.md) |
| `orchestrator` | List orchestrator sessions | Viewing which sessions are orchestrators | [commands/orchestrator.md](commands/orchestrator.md) |
| `review` | Start, list, cancel, or submit AO's native reviewer for a worker's PR (default: this session) | Getting an adversarial review of an AO session's PR; never spawn a worker to review | [commands/review.md](commands/review.md) |
| `send` | Send a message to a running agent session | Correcting or directing a live agent | [commands/send.md](commands/send.md) |
| `report` | Persist a meaningful worker report | Checkpoints, blockers, decisions, outputs, and completion | [commands/report.md](commands/report.md) |
| `preview` | Start a session-owned app or open an exact URL/file | Running and showing the worker's relevant app, Markdown, HTML, PDF, or image | [commands/preview.md](commands/preview.md) |
| `render` | Show a self-contained HTML page inline in a chat thread | Answering with a chart, table, diagram, or mockup | [commands/render.md](commands/render.md) |
| `browser` | Inspect and control the session's shared live browser | Verifying a web app through snapshots, interactions, waits, screenshots, console, and errors | [commands/browser.md](commands/browser.md) |
| `start` | Fetch (if needed) and open the AO desktop app | Launching the app | [commands/start.md](commands/start.md) |
| `stop` | Stop the AO daemon | Shutting down AO | [commands/stop.md](commands/stop.md) |
| `status` | Show daemon status | Verifying the daemon is up and healthy | [commands/status.md](commands/status.md) |
| `doctor` | Run local health checks | Diagnosing AO setup problems | [commands/doctor.md](commands/doctor.md) |
| `import` | Import projects from a legacy AO install | Migrating from the old flat-file store | [commands/import.md](commands/import.md) |
| `version` | Print version information | Checking installed version | - |
| `completion` | Generate shell completion scripts | Setting up tab completion | - |

## Conventions

- Most read commands accept `--json` for machine-readable output.
- `-p / --project` scopes session subcommand lookups to one project.
- Session and project ids are shown by `ao session ls` and `ao project ls`.
- To refer to a session in AO Chat or the AO terminal, use the canonical in-app
  link `ao://sessions/{project-id}/{session-id}`. Read
  [commands/session.md](commands/session.md) for identity, encoding, and safety
  rules before constructing one.
- When the user asks to save a repeatable task as a Cue, use `ao cue list --json` to check existing definitions, then `ao cue create`. An agent Cue stores a reusable instruction; a command Cue stores an exact shell command. This agent-facing command can create and read Cues, but cannot edit or delete them. Direct the user to project settings for changes to existing Cues.
- `--agent` is an alias for `--harness` on `ao spawn`.
- Every command accepts `-h / --help` for the full flag list.
- For frontend launch, preview selection, or artifact handoff, read
  [commands/preview.md](commands/preview.md) before acting. Its static-file,
  project-runtime, and automatic-handoff rules are load-bearing.
- For page inspection, interaction, or request diagnosis, read
  [commands/browser.md](commands/browser.md). It defines shared-tab behavior
  and the opt-in network policy.

Use [references.md](references.md) only when a natural-language request does
not map clearly to a command above.

description: "Catalog of the AO (Agent Orchestrator) `ao` CLI: spawning workers, managing sessions and projects, creating reusable Cues, sending messages, controlling the shared browser, previewing pages, and daemon control. Use when using the ao CLI, creating Cues, spawning workers, or managing AO sessions in an AO workspace."
trigger: "Using the ao CLI in an AO workspace: creating Cues, spawning workers, managing sessions/projects, sending messages, controlling or previewing pages."
---

# AO CLI Catalog

`ao` is a thin CLI over the local AO daemon. Every command is `ao <command> --help` for the authoritative flag list.

| Command | What it does | When to use | Details |
|---|---|---|---|
| `spawn` | Spawn a project worker, orchestrator, or projectless standalone worker | Starting a new task or issue | [commands/spawn.md](commands/spawn.md) |
| `session` | Manage agent sessions (list, kill, rename, restore, etc.) | Inspecting or controlling running/terminated sessions | [commands/session.md](commands/session.md) |
| `agent` | Inspect installed harnesses and launch readiness | Choosing or diagnosing an agent harness | `ao agent ls --refresh` |
| `pr` | Merge a PR or resolve its review threads | Completing a reviewed change | `ao pr merge` / `ao pr resolve-comments` |
| `project` | Register, inspect, configure, or remove projects | Setting up or managing repos AO knows about | [commands/project.md](commands/project.md) |
| `automation` | Manage durable recurring session automations | Creating, editing, disabling, deleting, and inspecting scheduled runs | [commands/automation.md](commands/automation.md) |
| `cue` | Create or list reusable project Cues | Saving a repetitive command or agent task at the user's request | [commands/cue.md](commands/cue.md) |
| `orchestrator` | List orchestrator sessions | Viewing which sessions are orchestrators | [commands/orchestrator.md](commands/orchestrator.md) |
| `review` | Start, list, cancel, or submit AO's native reviewer for a worker's PR (default: this session) | Getting an adversarial review of an AO session's PR; never spawn a worker to review | [commands/review.md](commands/review.md) |
| `send` | Send a message to a running agent session | Correcting or directing a live agent | [commands/send.md](commands/send.md) |
| `report` | Persist a meaningful worker report | Checkpoints, blockers, decisions, outputs, and completion | [commands/report.md](commands/report.md) |
| `preview` | Start a session-owned app or open an exact URL/file | Running and showing the worker's relevant app, Markdown, HTML, PDF, or image | [commands/preview.md](commands/preview.md) |
| `render` | Show a self-contained HTML page inline in a chat thread | Answering with a chart, table, diagram, or mockup | [commands/render.md](commands/render.md) |
| `browser` | Inspect and control the session's shared live browser | Verifying a web app through snapshots, interactions, waits, screenshots, console, and errors | [commands/browser.md](commands/browser.md) |
| `start` | Fetch (if needed) and open the AO desktop app | Launching the app | [commands/start.md](commands/start.md) |
| `stop` | Stop the AO daemon | Shutting down AO | [commands/stop.md](commands/stop.md) |
| `status` | Show daemon status | Verifying the daemon is up and healthy | [commands/status.md](commands/status.md) |
| `doctor` | Run local health checks | Diagnosing AO setup problems | [commands/doctor.md](commands/doctor.md) |
| `import` | Import projects from a legacy AO install | Migrating from the old flat-file store | [commands/import.md](commands/import.md) |
| `version` | Print version information | Checking installed version | - |
| `completion` | Generate shell completion scripts | Setting up tab completion | - |

## Conventions

- Most read commands accept `--json` for machine-readable output.
- `-p / --project` scopes session subcommand lookups to one project.
- Session and project ids are shown by `ao session ls` and `ao project ls`.
- To refer to a session in AO Chat or the AO terminal, use the canonical in-app
  link `ao://sessions/{project-id}/{session-id}`. Read
  [commands/session.md](commands/session.md) for identity, encoding, and safety
  rules before constructing one.
- When the user asks to save a repeatable task as a Cue, use `ao cue list --json` to check existing definitions, then `ao cue create`. An agent Cue stores a reusable instruction; a command Cue stores an exact shell command. This agent-facing command can create and read Cues, but cannot edit or delete them. Direct the user to project settings for changes to existing Cues.
- `--agent` is an alias for `--harness` on `ao spawn`.
- Every command accepts `-h / --help` for the full flag list.
- For frontend launch, preview selection, or artifact handoff, read
  [commands/preview.md](commands/preview.md) before acting. Its static-file,
  project-runtime, and automatic-handoff rules are load-bearing.
- For page inspection, interaction, or request diagnosis, read
  [commands/browser.md](commands/browser.md). It defines shared-tab behavior
  and the opt-in network policy.

Use [references.md](references.md) only when a natural-language request does

item.stdout:
# ao session

Manage agent sessions: list, inspect, rename, kill, restore, exit or resume an
agent, switch harnesses, clean up, and claim PRs.

## In-app session links

When referring a user or another agent to a session in AO Chat or the AO
terminal, emit this canonical link:

```text
ao://sessions/{project-id}/{session-id}
```

- Use stable IDs returned by `ao project ls` and `ao session ls`, or the current
  session's `AO_PROJECT_ID` and `AO_SESSION_ID`. Never use display names as
  identity; renaming a session must not change its link.
- Treat the project ID and session ID as separate URL path segments. Encode
  either ID with URL percent encoding if it contains characters that are not
  safe in one segment.
- Emit only the navigation route above. Do not append query strings, fragments,
  action names, credentials, authorities, or extra path segments.
- The link is handled only inside a currently running AO desktop app. It is not
  an operating-system protocol link and must not be described as supporting
  cold launch or navigation from external applications.
- A session link navigates; it never sends a message, executes a command, or
  performs another action.

Example for project `mercury` and session `mer-3`:

```text
ao://sessions/mercury/mer-3
```

## Syntax

```
ao session <subcommand> [args] [flags]
```

## Subcommands

---

### ao session ls

List sessions.

**Syntax:**
```
ao session ls [flags]
```

**Flags:**

| Flag | Meaning | Default / Required |
|---|---|---|
| `-a, --all` | Include orchestrator sessions | - |

Manage agent sessions: list, inspect, rename, kill, restore, exit or resume an
agent, switch harnesses, clean up, and claim PRs.

## In-app session links

When referring a user or another agent to a session in AO Chat or the AO
terminal, emit this canonical link:

```text
ao://sessions/{project-id}/{session-id}
```

- Use stable IDs returned by `ao project ls` and `ao session ls`, or the current
  session's `AO_PROJECT_ID` and `AO_SESSION_ID`. Never use display names as
  identity; renaming a session must not change its link.
- Treat the project ID and session ID as separate URL path segments. Encode
  either ID with URL percent encoding if it contains characters that are not
  safe in one segment.
- Emit only the navigation route above. Do not append query strings, fragments,
  action names, credentials, authorities, or extra path segments.
- The link is handled only inside a currently running AO desktop app. It is not
  an operating-system protocol link and must not be described as supporting
  cold launch or navigation from external applications.
- A session link navigates; it never sends a message, executes a command, or
  performs another action.

Example for project `mercury` and session `mer-3`:

```text
ao://sessions/mercury/mer-3
```

## Syntax

```
ao session <subcommand> [args] [flags]
```

## Subcommands

---

### ao session ls

List sessions.

**Syntax:**
```
ao session ls [flags]
```

**Flags:**

| Flag | Meaning | Default / Required |
|---|---|---|
| `-a, --all` | Include orchestrator sessions | - |
| `--include-terminated` | Include terminated sessions | - |
| `--json` | Output as JSON | - |
| `-p, --project string` | Filter by project ID | - |

**Examples:**

```bash
# List all active worker sessions
ao session ls
```

```bash
# List all sessions including terminated, scoped to one project
ao session ls --include-terminated -p agent-orchestrator
```

---

### ao session get

Fetch one session.

**Syntax:**
```
ao session get <id> [flags]
```

**Flags:**

| Flag | Meaning | Default / Required |
|---|---|---|
| `--json` | Output as JSON | - |
| `-p, --project string` | Project id to scope the lookup | - |

**Examples:**

```bash
# Get details for session mer-3
ao session get mer-3
```

```bash
# Get session details as JSON
ao session get mer-3 --json
```

---

### ao session kill

Terminate a session.

**Syntax:**
```
ao session kill <id> [flags]
```

**Flags:**

| Flag | Meaning | Default / Required |
|---|---|---|
| `-p, --project string` | Project id to scope the lookup | - |

**Examples:**

```bash
# Kill session mer-3
ao session kill mer-3
```

---

### ao session rename

Rename a worker session. The project orchestrator cannot be renamed, including by itself; the daemon refuses with `ORCHESTRATOR_RENAME_UNSUPPORTED`.

**Syntax:**
```
ao session rename <id> <name> [flags]
```

**Flags:**

| Flag | Meaning | Default / Required |
|---|---|---|
| `-p, --project string` | Project id to scope the lookup | - |

**Examples:**

```bash
# Rename session mer-3 to a new display name
ao session rename mer-3 "fix-auth-bug"
```

---

### ao session restore

Restore a terminated session or resume an exited agent.

**Syntax:**
```
ao session restore <id> [flags]
```

**Flags:**

| Flag | Meaning | Default / Required |
|---|---|---|
| `-p, --project string` | Project id to scope the lookup | - |

**Examples:**

```bash
# Restore a terminated session
ao session restore mer-3
```

---

### ao session exit-agent

Exit an agent without terminating its AO session. The session can later be
resumed in place.

**Syntax:**
```
ao session exit-agent <id> [flags]
```

**Flags:**

| Flag | Meaning | Default / Required |
|---|---|---|
| `--json` | Output as JSON | - |
| `-p, --project string` | Project id to scope the lookup | - |

---

### ao session resume-agent

Resume an exited agent in its existing AO session.

**Syntax:**
```
ao session resume-agent <id> [flags]
```

**Flags:**

| Flag | Meaning | Default / Required |
|---|---|---|
| `--json` | Output as JSON | - |
| `-p, --project string` | Project id to scope the lookup | - |

**Examples:**

```bash
ao session exit-agent mer-3
ao session resume-agent mer-3
```

---

### ao session switch-agent

Switch a running session to another installed agent harness. This preserves the
AO session while provisioning the target harness.

**Syntax:**
```
ao session switch-agent <id> <target-harness> [flags]
```

**Flags:**

| Flag | Meaning | Default / Required |
|---|---|---|
| `--idempotency-key string` | Reuse a prior identical switch request safely | - |
| `--json` | Output the agent switch as JSON | - |

**Examples:**

```bash
ao session switch-agent mer-3 codex
```

---

### ao session agent-switch ls

List agent-harness switches recorded for a session. Alias: `agent-switches`.

**Syntax:**
```
ao session agent-switch ls <session-id> [flags]
```

**Flags:**

| Flag | Meaning | Default / Required |
|---|---|---|
| `--json` | Output agent switches as JSON | - |

**Examples:**

```bash
ao session agent-switch ls mer-3
```

---

### ao session cleanup

Clean up terminated sessions by reclaiming eligible workspaces. Dirty worktrees are skipped by the daemon.

**Syntax:**
```
ao session cleanup [flags]
```

**Flags:**

| Flag | Meaning | Default / Required |
|---|---|---|
| `--dry-run` | Preview which sessions would be cleaned without removing anything | - |
| `-p, --project string` | Filter by project ID | - |
| `-y, --yes` | Skip confirmation prompt | - |

**Examples:**

```bash
# Clean up all terminated sessions (skip prompt)
ao session cleanup -y
```

```bash
# Clean up terminated sessions for one project
ao session cleanup -p agent-orchestrator
```

```bash
# Preview eligible cleanup candidates
ao session cleanup --dry-run
```

---

### ao session claim-pr

Attach an existing PR to the current AO session, or target another session explicitly.

**Syntax:**
```
ao session claim-pr <pr-ref> [flags]
ao session claim-pr <session-id> <pr-ref> [flags]
```

With one positional argument, `AO_SESSION_ID` supplies the session. This is the preferred form inside a worker. Pass both arguments from an orchestrator or external shell when targeting another session.

**Flags:**

| Flag | Meaning | Default / Required |
|---|---|---|
| `--json` | Output as JSON | - |
| `--no-takeover` | Refuse if another active session owns the PR | - |
| `-p, --project string` | Project id to scope the lookup | - |

**Examples:**

```bash
# Attach PR 88 to the current worker session
ao session claim-pr 88
```

```bash
# Attach PR 88 to session mer-3 explicitly
ao session claim-pr mer-3 88
```

```bash
# Claim PR 88 for the current worker but refuse if another session owns it
ao session claim-pr 88 --no-takeover
```

# ao report

Persist a meaningful worker report for durable delivery to the active project
orchestrator.

## Syntax

```text
ao report <free-form-text>
ao report --checkpoint --note <text> [output flags]
ao report --needs-input --note <text> [output flags]
ao report --stuck --note <text> [output flags]
ao report --done --note <text> [output flags]
```

Output flags are repeatable:

```text
--artifact <opaque-reference>
--pr-created <pr-or-mr-url>
--pr-reviewed <pr-or-mr-url>
```

Use reports for meaningful transitions, decisions, blockers, required input,
outputs, and terminal judgment. Do not narrate routine commands. Outputs do not
imply completion, and `--done` does not terminate the session.

Attach a reviewable deliverable as soon as it is ready, not only at `--done`:
use `--artifact <reference>` on the report for the milestone that produced it.
Examples include a requested document, a rendered dashboard, or another output
the orchestrator or human needs to open directly. `--artifact` takes any opaque
reference string; it is not validated as a URL.
In a chat session, an HTML file from the artifact directory that you attach
with `--artifact` also shows in the thread.

Routine test logs, command output, scratch notes, and intermediate diagnostics
are working material, not deliverables. Do not attach them unless requested or
needed to explain an actionable failure. Summarize validation in the report note;
when a separate deliverable is useful, prefer one consolidated report over
individual logs. Ordinary progress updates and concise final answers do not
need separate artifact files.

Saving a local artifact or attaching its reference to an AO report is not
external publishing authorization. Publish externally only within the
user-authorized scope.

`--pr-created` and `--pr-reviewed` accept complete GitHub PR or GitLab MR URLs.

`--needs-input` requests immediate non-interrupting delivery. `--stuck`
requests immediate delivery plus a rate-limited interrupt. Informational work
batches for up to one hour, while the first done report opens a fixed five
minute settlement window.

**Examples:**

```bash
ao report "The focused tests pass; I am checking the generated diff."
ao report --done --note "Ready for review." \
  --pr-created https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/88
```

# Escalation Requests

Commands are run outside the sandbox if they are approved by the user, or match an existing rule that allows it to run unrestricted. The command string is split into independent command segments at shell control operators, including but not limited to:

- Pipes: |
- Logical operators: &&, ||
- Command separators: ;
- Subshell boundaries: (...), $(...)

Each resulting segment is evaluated independently for sandbox restrictions and approval requirements.

Example:

git pull | tee output.txt

This is treated as two command segments:

["git", "pull"]

["tee", "output.txt"]

Commands that use more advanced shell features like redirection (>, >>, <), substitutions ($(...), ...), environment variables (FOO=bar), or wildcard patterns (*, ?) will not be evaluated against rules, to limit the scope of what an approved rule allows.

## How to request escalation

IMPORTANT: To request approval to execute a command that will require escalated privileges:

- Provide the `sandbox_permissions` parameter with the value `"require_escalated"`
- Include a short question asking the user if they want to allow the action in `justification` parameter. e.g. "Do you want to download and install dependencies for this project?"

## When to request escalation

While commands are running inside the sandbox, here are some scenarios that will require escalation outside the sandbox:

- You need to run a command that writes to a directory that requires it (e.g. running tests that write to /var)

## prefix_rule guidance

# Escalation Requests

Commands are run outside the sandbox if they are approved by the user, or match an existing rule that allows it to run unrestricted. The command string is split into independent command segments at shell control operators, including but not limited to:

- Pipes: |
- Logical operators: &&, ||
- Command separators: ;
- Subshell boundaries: (...), $(...)

Each resulting segment is evaluated independently for sandbox restrictions and approval requirements.

Example:

git pull | tee output.txt

This is treated as two command segments:

["git", "pull"]

["tee", "output.txt"]

Commands that use more advanced shell features like redirection (>, >>, <), substitutions ($(...), ...), environment variables (FOO=bar), or wildcard patterns (*, ?) will not be evaluated against rules, to limit the scope of what an approved rule allows.

## How to request escalation

IMPORTANT: To request approval to execute a command that will require escalated privileges:

- Provide the `sandbox_permissions` parameter with the value `"require_escalated"`
- Include a short question asking the user if they want to allow the action in `justification` parameter. e.g. "Do you want to download and install dependencies for this project?"

## When to request escalation

While commands are running inside the sandbox, here are some scenarios that will require escalation outside the sandbox:

- You need to run a command that writes to a directory that requires it (e.g. running tests that write to /var)

## prefix_rule guidance

L254: # Entire CLI
L255: 
L256: Entire hooks into your Git workflow to capture AI agent sessions as you work. Sessions are indexed alongside commits, creating a searchable record of how code was written in your repo.
L257: 
L258: With Entire, you can:
L259:   * Understand why code changed — see the full prompt/response transcript and files touched
L260:   * Pick up where you left off — resume an agent session and its conversation from a checkpoint
L261:   * Keep Git history clean — agent context lives outside your branch's history
L262:   * Onboard faster — show the path from prompt → change → commit
L263:   * Maintain traceability — support audit and compliance requirements when needed
L264: ## Why Entire
L265:   * Understand why code changed, not just what — Transcripts, prompts, files touched, token usage, tool calls, and more are captured alongside every commit.
L266:   * Resume from any checkpoint — Go back to any previous agent session and pick up exactly where you or a coworker left off.
L267:   * Full context preserved and searchable — A versioned record of every AI interaction tied to your git history, with nothing lost.

L297: ## Quick Start
L298: ### macOS and Linux
L299: 
L300: Install with Homebrew:
L301: 
L302:     brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire
L303: 
L304: Use the fully-qualified cask name (`entireio/tap/entire`, not `entire`). Homebrew 6 requires third-party taps to be trusted before it will evaluate them, and a fully-qualified name taps and trusts just that one cask, so no separate `brew tap` / `brew trust` step is needed. Requires Homebrew 6.0.10 or newer.
L305: Or with the install script:
L306: 
L307:     curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash                          # stable
L308:     # curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly  # or nightly
L309: ### Windows
L310: 
L311: Install with Windows PowerShell 5.1 or later:
L312: 
L313:     irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 | iex  # stable
L314:     # or nightly:
L315:     # iex "& {$(irm https://entire.io/install.ps1)} -Channel nightly"
L316: For stable releases, the PowerShell installer uses Scoop when it is available, adding the Entire bucket if needed. Without Scoop — and for nightly releases — it verifies the release checksum and installs both `entire.exe` and `git-remote-entire.exe` to `%USERPROFILE%\.local\bin`, adding that directory to your user `PATH` if needed.
L317: 
L318: Or install the stable release with Scoop:
L319: 
L320:     scoop bucket add entire https://github.com/entireio/scoop-bucket.git
L321:     scoop install entire/entire
L322: #### Migrating an old `cli` Scoop install (package rename)
L323: The Scoop package was renamed from `cli` to `entire`. If your install is still registered as the old `cli` package, run the migration below. It installs the new package before removing the old one, so the old install is only removed once the new one is in place (`scoop reset` re-links the shared `entire.exe` and `git-remote-entire.exe` shims). Run it where `entire` is not running — a live `entire.exe` locks its own shim, so Scoop can't relink or uninstall it mid-run:
L324:     cmd.exe /D /C "scoop install entire/entire && scoop uninstall entire/cli && scoop reset entire"
L325: If the first step fails with "couldn't find manifest", your bucket clone predates the renamed package — run `scoop update` to refresh it, then retry the command above. Nothing is removed until the install succeeds, so a failed attempt leaves your existing install working.
L326: ### Go (development/manual setup)
L327: 
L328:     go install github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire@latest
L329: 
L330:     # The git remote helper that resolves entire:// URLs, needed for `entire repo clone`
L331:     # and `git clone entire://…`. The packaged installs above bundle it.
L332:     go install github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/git-remote-entire@latest
L333: 
L334:     # Add Go binaries to PATH (add to ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc if not already configured)
L335:     export PATH="$HOME/go/bin:$PATH"
L336: Install both, or just `entire` if you never clone over `entire://`. Git finds the helper by name on `$PATH`, which is what `go install` produces, so nothing else needs configuring.
L337: 
L338: One difference from a stable release: a `go install` build leaves cite150†experimental commands visible in `entire help`, the same as a nightly or a local build.
L339: ### Enable in your project
L340: 
L341:     cd your-project && entire enable
L342: 
L343:     # Check status
L344:     entire status
L345: 
L346: After the initial setup, use `entire agent` to add or remove agents, `entire configure` to update non-agent settings, and `entire enable` / `entire disable` to toggle Entire on or off.
L347: ## Release Channels
L348: 
L349: Entire currently ships two release channels:
L350: 
L351:   * `stable`: recommended for most users. Stable releases change less often and are the default for Homebrew, Scoop, and `install.sh`.
L352:   * `nightly`: prerelease builds for users who want the latest changes earlier. Nightlies are published more frequently and may include newer, less-proven changes than stable.
L353: 
L354: How to use each channel:
L355:   * Homebrew stable: `brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire`
L356:   * Homebrew nightly: `brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire@nightly`
L357:   * `install.sh` stable: `curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash`
L358:   * `install.sh` nightly: `curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly`
L359:   * `install.ps1` stable (uses Scoop when available): `irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 | iex`
L360:   * `install.ps1` nightly: `iex "& {$(irm https://entire.io/install.ps1)} -Channel nightly"`
L361:   * Scoop: currently supports `stable` only via `scoop install entire/entire`
L362: ## Typical Workflow
L363: ### 1. Enable Entire in Your Repository
L364: 
L365:     `entire enable
L366:     `
L367: 
L368: On a repo that has not been enabled yet, `entire enable` runs the initial enable flow: it creates Entire settings, installs git hooks, and prompts you to choose which agent hooks to install. To enable a specific agent non-interactively, use `entire enable --agent <name>` (for example, `entire enable --agent cursor`).
L369: 
L370: After setup:
L371:   * Use `entire enable` to turn Entire back on if the repo is currently disabled.
L372:   * Use `entire agent` to add or remove agents.
L373:   * Use `entire configure` to update non-agent settings (telemetry, hooks, checkpoint remote, summary provider).
L374: The hooks capture session data as you work. Checkpoints are created when you or the agent make a git commit. Your code commits stay clean, Entire never creates commits on your active branch. Session metadata is stored outside your branch's history, in the checkpoint storage described under cite137†Checkpoint Storage .
L375: #### Existing git hooks
L376: 
L377: If your repository already has git hooks (your own scripts, git-lfs, lefthook, pre-commit), `entire enable` keeps them: each one is moved to `<hook>.pre-entire` in the hooks directory, and Entire's hook runs first, then yours.
L378:   * If a hook manager reinstalls its hooks later, Entire's hooks come back on the next agent turn or `entire enable`, chained to the hook manager's version. If the hook already had a `<hook>.pre-entire` copy, the hook manager's version takes its place and runs after Entire's; the older copy is kept as `<hook>.pre-entire.<timestamp>` and no longer runs, with a warning naming the file.

# Tally

A CFO for a fleet of coding agents. Give it a backlog and a budget. It sizes
each task, sends it to the cheapest model likely to finish it, stops any task
that overruns its spend ceiling, hands failed work to a stronger model, and
ends with a ledger tying every dollar to a merged PR.

Status: early build. The shared data contract exists, `tally demo` runs the
seven-task simulated demo backlog, and `tally run --dry-run` writes run state
plus a ledger from a file-backed backlog. The real AO worker path is wired and
ready for a gated one-task smoke run.

## Install

Prerequisites before you install:

- Node 20 or later.
- Agent Orchestrator installed and running.
- At least one signed-in coding agent that Agent Orchestrator can start.
- GitHub CLI installed and signed in with `gh auth login`.

Three ways in:

```bash
npm install -g github:Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack
npm install -g tally-agents
git clone https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack && cd neatlogs-hack && npm install && npm run build
```

The npm package is named `tally-agents`; the installed command is still
`tally`.

## Quickstart

Needs Node 20 or later.

```bash
npm install
npm run build
npm run tally -- demo --dashboard
npm run tally -- demo --live --dashboard
npm run tally -- dashboard
npm run tally -- doctor --config demo/tally.yaml
npm run tally -- run --dry-run --plan --config demo/tally.yaml
npm run tally -- login cfoai
npm run tally -- market --limit 5
```

The first two commands install and compile Tally. The remaining commands show
the full fake-worker demo, the read-only live-integration demo, the standalone
dashboard, integration checks, a dry-run plan, cfo.ai login, and the CrustData
market search. Run them one at a time; dashboard commands keep serving until
you stop them. Commands that call external services report the missing login or
API key instead of printing secrets. During development, `npm run tally --
<command>` runs the CLI from source. After `npm run build`,
`node bin/tally.js <command>` runs the compiled package entry.

For routine validation, run:

```bash
npm test
```

## Commands

| Command | What it will do |
|---|---|
| `tally run` | Run the backlog against the budget in `tally.yaml`. Flags: `--dry-run`, `--budget <usd>`, `--only <task>`, `--baseline`, `--config <path>`, `--plan`, `--dashboard`/`--open`. |
| `tally demo` | Run the full loop with simulated workers on `demo/tally.yaml` and `demo/sample-backlog.yaml`. No accounts or keys. Writes `.tally/runs/<run-id>/run.json` and `ledger.json`; add `--dashboard` for the one-command demo, or `--live` to light up read-only integrations while workers stay fake. |
| `tally dashboard` | Serve `dashboard/` and `.tally/runs/` read-only on `127.0.0.1`. The printed URL passes `?data=/runs/latest/` so the page reads the stable latest-run mirror. |
| `tally init` | Detect the test command, ask for a budget and issue label, and write `tally.yaml`. |
| `tally doctor` | One line per integration: connected, missing or broken, with the fix. |

## Layout

| Folder | Holds |
|---|---|
| `schema/` | The contract every part reads: TypeScript types, JSON Schema, validators, and a sample finished run in `schema/fixtures/finished-run/`. |
| `engine/` | The run loop, run state and ledger. |
| `adapters/` | One thin module per outside tool (Agent Orchestrator, Entire, neatlogs, cfo.ai, GitHub). |
| `agent/` | The CFO agent: sizing, routing, ceilings, escalation. |
| `cli/` | The `tally` command. |
| `dashboard/` | Static page that reads the ledger and run state. |
| `demo/` | Sample backlog and scripted outcomes for `tally demo`. |

## Configuration

Tally assumes nothing about the repository it works on. The repository, test
command, model tiers, list prices, ceilings and budget all come from
`tally.yaml` (a tier is a name, harness, model id, provider, list price and ceiling share); see `schema/fixtures/finished-run/tally.yaml` for a complete

[from neatlogs-hack-8] From the orchestrator. After your checkpoint PR, one more item for you, requested by the human: the dashboard will draw the slice of Entire's code graph that Tally used to size each task, updating live. Lane C draws it; you supply the data. Data contract (agreed between lanes B and C; lane B writes it, lane C draws it). Each task in run.json gains an optional 'impact' object, written when the task is sized and never changed afterwards: { source: 'entire-graph' | 'code-search' | 'scripted' | 'none', query: string (the search text used), nodes: [{ id: string (repo-relative file path), kind: 'target' | 'caller' | 'coChange' | 'test', symbol?: string, weight?: number }], edges: [{ from: id, to: id, kind: 'calls' | 'changesWith' | 'tests' }], totals: { filesTouched, dependents, testsPresent }, truncated: boolean }. Cap at 40 nodes and 80 edges per task, keeping the highest-weight ones and setting truncated true when anything was dropped; totals always carry the full counts. After the worker finishes, the task also gains 'changedFiles': [repo-relative paths] taken from the diff of the worker branch against its base, so the picture can show what was predicted against what was actually edited.

Your part, in adapters/entire.ts and the sizing path, one PR from the latest origin/main: 1. EntireSizingAdapter already runs graph search then impact on the top symbols; keep what it learns instead of collapsing it to three numbers. Record the files of the target symbols as 'target', direct callers' files as 'caller', co-change files as 'coChange', and test files as 'test', with edges, per the contract. Paths repo-relative, never absolute. The code-search fallback fills targets only with source 'code-search'; dry runs with scripted sizing write source 'scripted' with whatever the sample provides. 2. tasks:
  - id: FDJ-1
    issueNumber: 1
    issueUrl: https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/fly-doom-jev/issues/1
    title: Add replay loader coverage for malformed recording files
    size: small
    label: tally
    body: |
      The replay loader already rejects a recording with no header, but it does
      not have focused coverage for malformed JSONL rows or frame metadata with
      a missing pattern. Add defensive tests and the smallest loader changes
      needed so a bad recording reports a clear exception instead of failing
      later in the API.
    passCheck: .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/unit/test_recording.py -q

  - id: FDJ-2
    issueNumber: 2
    issueUrl: https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/fly-doom-jev/issues/2
    title: Include goal fields in encoded state tests
    size: small
    label: tally
    body: |
      `EnvironmentState` has a `goal` field for E1M1 strategy, but the unit
      tests only assert the older threat and serialization fields. Add coverage
      proving that a goal dict can be attached, serialized, and omitted for
      ordinary arena observations without breaking the existing schema version.
    passCheck: .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/unit/test_state_encoder.py -q

  - id: FDJ-3
    issueNumber: 3
    issueUrl: https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/fly-doom-jev/issues/3
    title: Test POST /new rejects unknown live scenarios
    size: small
    label: tally
    body: |
      The live API validates scenario names in `request_new_episode`, but there
      is no direct API-level test for a bad `POST /new` body. Add a small test
      around the FastAPI route or the loop method so an unknown scenario returns
      a clear error and leaves the current scenario unchanged.
    passCheck: .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/unit/test_jev_live.py -q

  - id: FDJ-4
    issueNumber: 4
    issueUrl: https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/fly-doom-jev/issues/4
    title: Preserve recording summary when both summary and episode_end rows exist
    size: medium
    label: tally
    body: |
      `load_recording` treats both `summary` and `episode_end` rows as the
      recording summary. Make the behavior explicit and deterministic when a
      file contains both rows, then add a regression test that documents which
      one wins and why. Keep the public replay response shape unchanged.
    passCheck: .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/unit/test_recording.py tests/integration/test_closed_loop.py -q

  - id: FDJ-5
    issueNumber: 5
    issueUrl: https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/fly-doom-jev/issues/5
    title: Add action-weighting regression for missing MOVEMENT_INTENT metadata
    size: medium
    label: tally
    body: |
      `jev_action_weights` reads optional movement-intent probabilities from
      decision metadata. Add coverage for decisions that have probabilities but
      no `choice_probabilities` key, and make the implementation tolerate that
      shape without changing the existing weighting semantics.
    passCheck: .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/unit/test_weighting.py tests/unit/test_jev.py -q

  - id: FDJ-6
    issueNumber: 6
    issueUrl: https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/fly-doom-jev/issues/6
    title: Make plasticity checkpoint errors actionable
    size: medium
    label: tally
    body: |
      A corrupt or incompatible plasticity checkpoint should fail with a message
      that names the checkpoint path and provenance mismatch instead of a raw
      NumPy exception. Add tests for corrupt checkpoint data and mismatched
      config hashes, then keep the fresh-start fallback for ordinary provenance
      mismatch.
    passCheck: .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/unit/test_plasticity.py -q

  - id: FDJ-7
    issueNumber: 7
    issueUrl: https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/fly-doom-jev/issues/7
    title: Add deterministic featured-recording generation for the static showcase
    size: medium
    difficultyNote: looks medium but is hard
    label: tally
    body: |
      The project now serves a static GitHub Pages showcase from curated
      recordings. Add a deterministic packaging path that writes `featured.json`
      in a stable order, verifies every referenced recording and frame exists,
      and fails loudly when a curated bundle is incomplete. This looks medium
      because it is packaging code, but it crosses replay metadata, static
      assets, and CLI behavior.
    passCheck: .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/unit/test_recording.py tests/unit/test_hf_export.py -q

Requested by the human on 11 Oct. He asked where he could see the graphs Entire creates. Entire's code graph has no visual at all; it is CLI and JSON only. So Tally's dashboard draws it: for each task, the slice of the code graph Tally used to size that task.

He was explicit on two points:

1. It must be properly designed, not a chart dropped onto the page.
2. It must change in real time.

## Data contract

Agreed between lanes B and C. Lane B writes it, lane C draws it.

Each task in `run.json` gains an optional `impact` object, written when the task is sized and never changed afterwards:

```json
{
  "source": "entire-graph | code-search | scripted | none",
  "query": "the search text used",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "repo-relative/file/path.py", "kind": "target | caller | coChange | test", "symbol": "optional", "weight": 1 }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "node id", "to": "node id", "kind": "calls | changesWith | tests" }
  ],
  "totals": { "filesTouched": 2, "dependents": 5, "testsPresent": true },
  "truncated": false
}
```

- At most 40 nodes and 80 edges per task. Keep the highest-weight ones and set `truncated` to true when anything was dropped. `totals` always carries the full counts.
- Paths are repo-relative, never absolute.
- After the worker finishes, the task also gains `changedFiles`: an array of repo-relative paths, from the diff of the worker branch against its base. This lets the picture show what was predicted against what was actually edited.

## What lane C builds

In `dashboard/` only. Static page, no framework, no charting library, hand-written inline SVG.

### Where it lives

Inside each task, opened from the task row. The row already carries the "why" sentence and the files-touched and dependents numbers. The numbers stay as the summary; the picture is the explanation beneath them. Do not add a separate graph page or a generic network diagram at the top of the page.

### What it shows

The files the task is expected to touch at the centre, and what depends on them around that: callers, files that change together, tests. The reading is "this is why Tally called the task small, medium or large".

A viewer should understand it in five seconds without hunting for a legend:

- direct labels on the nodes that matter;
- a one-line caption stating the totals and the size they led to;
- an honest "showing 40 of N" when truncated.

### Layout

Deterministic: the same input always gives the same picture, so nothing jumps between polls. A layered or radial layout computed in plain JS. No force simulation, no random jitter. Long paths are shortened in the middle, with the full path available on hover and to screen readers.

### Design

It must belong to the existing page:

- the same ink-on-paper language and the same type;
- the single red accent used only for what needs attention: a stopped attempt, or a file edited outside the predicted set;
- line weight and node shape carry the rest, not a rainbow of colours;
- works in print and at 390 px width;
- never relies on colour alone.

### Real time

The page already polls `run.json` and `ledger.json`. As a run proceeds the picture updates in place, without redrawing from scratch:

1. a task appears when it is sized;
2. its target files mark as the attempt runs;
3. a stopped or failed attempt shows on the same picture, and the escalated attempt continues it;
4. when the worker finishes, the files it actually changed are marked, and any changed file outside the predicted set is called out.

Transitions are short and calm. Honour `prefers-reduced-motion` with no animation at all.

### States

- No impact data (older runs, or the product switched off): show nothing, not an empty box.
- `scripted` sample data is labelled as sample.
- A task with one file and no dependents still looks intentional.

### How to build and check it

Build it now against a hand-made fixture that follows the contract exactly, including a run that changes over time (use the existing replay mechanism), so it is ready the moment lane B's real data lands.

Before reporting, look at it rendered at desktop and phone width and say what was checked. The orchestrator reviews the rendered page before merging. One PR.
